rows.postTitle: Re: Re: Re: Pritchard On Liberal Happiness
rows.text: Yeah. Prosperity, national product, national wealth. The term has changed but economic expansion has been a political object since before the US was a country. The American Revolutionaries were writing about economic restrictions. Franklin has a very sarcastic letter about British restrictions on American industry.

rows.postTitle: Re: Re: Re: Pritchard On Liberal Happiness
rows.text: Yeah. So did Hamilton. Jefferson and Hamilton were partly arguing over which way of organizing the economy would create more wealth with Jefferson eventually arguing that even if his way didn't it was better for democracy. Though he never quite gave up the idea his way was better economically. Pursuit of happiness is a direct reference to property because they didn't want to use the word property because it was felt to be a reference to slaves. Etc.

Now then, you've moved beyond the claim that was made (that it happens) to a strawman (that it was substantial portion of their funding). I am not going to answer for a claim that was not made. You are welcome to reread what I said here or elsewhere in the thread. What has been said is it was "a factor" and I only claimed it existed.

As to the claim I did make:

Eileen Wang is the most recent. She plead guilty to acting as a foreign agent for the PRC while being a politician and part of that was fundraising for various left wing causes. (Though she was a Republican before becoming an agent. Apparently she was encouraged to switch.) The real story is not her so much as the man caught with her who recruited her who was more central to California Democratic politics.

There's also the Singham network which is currently under investigation.

There's also the various aides and drivers and such found (mostly among Democrats and leftists) to have aided them in fundraising, including money laundering, while also spying on them. (Note this means the principal/progressive candidate did not know. Which is common.)

The whole CUSEF network (which was mostly Democrat but partly bipartisan). The Clinton Foundation ties. The Code Pink funding (which is Singham). The NYC Hometown Networks, several of whom leaned progressive and almost all left wing.

And in the 1990s there's the Thompson investigation into interference in the 1996 election. Which was a massive scandal with multiple convictions mostly in California and NY (or nearby). In between there's been a steady drumbeat of such things. And possibly earlier though I'm less familiar with pre-1996.

I'm also skipping things like the LA-Shenzhen network and other such groups. That did happen and it was left wing but I tend to see that as more ordinary business corruption. They gave millions to left wing politicians but they (to me) appear to be private businessmen seeking quid pro quo for construction approvals. If you count that though there's a bunch of those too in several major cities (again California and NY concentrated).

The Congressional Progressive Caucus has been around since the 1990s. We forget this but the AOC route of radical->mainstream has a bunch of antecedents. A lot of this playbook actually comes out of the original PC era. The Democrat Party hasn't so much gained a larger left flank as lost its right flank. I mean there's been a slight increase but from ~77 to ~96 representatives. Same with other offices.

If you mean the DSA a lot of that was Bernie. His presidential run failed but he built significant infrastructure. At the same time progressive funding (Soros but also less famous backers like Jurvetson or Hoffman) became more radical and more willing to back outright social candidates. So there was a machine to absorb money and elite backers willing to pour in money. Which is how this works. Political influence comes from people putting in the legwork but money lets them do it professionally.

Despite this, in my view, the DSA/socialists actually underperformed. Pelosi's comment a glass of water with a D next to it could win in New York and that the Squad is four people remain true. New York has always been the DSA heartland anyway and their wins were mostly in deep blue areas of NY, PA, and MI. And one in Colorado. But there's a well heeled staffer class and they're very good at social media. Unfortunately many of them are not very good at, uh, politics. They have significant issues with bubble thinking and in translating that money into broad victories, partly due to litmus tests. And this is currently driving a split between the relatively more pragmatic AOC and Jayapal types and the radical to their left.

But the consensus news cycle, even among progressives, has been that the DSA and socialists have underperformed. (The socialists insist they did well against expectations and/or the mainstream party sabotaged them.) I think it's partly due to bad candidate quality in some races. Platner and Hong most famously. Platner in particular caused some significant dressing downs of the more radical progressives. But it's also just they're not as popular as some people imagine. El-Sayed, who is also underperforming, notably avoids the label entirely. The entire "wave" is like seven people in deep blue seats and that assumes they all win their generals.
